cloze.text: A potassium nitrate desensitizing toothpaste requires consistent use for {{c1::2+ weeks}} before effects are noticed.
Peroxide dentifrices are used for {{c1::whitening}} of both extrinsic and intrinsic stains; they break down stain molecules through {{c2::oxidation}}.
cloze.extra: Brand examples: Crest 3D White, Colgate Optic White.

cloze.text: Peroxide toothpastes are primarily cosmetic and may cause {{c1::tissue irritation or transient sensitivity}}.
In CPP-ACP, a {{c1::casein-derived protein}} stabilizes {{c2::calcium and phosphate}} ions to support remineralization.
cloze.extra: Brand examples: MI Paste, MI Paste Plus.

cloze.text: CPP-ACP promotes {{c1::reversal of early lesions}} and helps buffer acids, but it is {{c2::not a fluoride source}}.

{{c1::Triclosan}} is a broad-spectrum antibacterial dentifrice agent (anti-gingivitis, anti-plaque) that was {{c2::removed from many U.S. products over safety concerns}}; it is still seen internationally.
{{c1::Pyrophosphate}} dentifrices control calculus by preventing {{c2::crystal growth in supragingival plaque}}.
cloze.extra: Brand example: Crest Tartar Protection. Book: may cause sensitivity or tissue irritation in some users.

cloze.text: A side effect of pyrophosphate (tartar-control) toothpaste in some users is {{c1::sensitivity or tissue irritation}}.
Fluoride varnish (5% NaF) has a {{c1::neutral}} pH and is indicated for high caries risk at all ages and for {{c2::sensitivity}}.
Fluoride varnish needs {{c1::no prophylaxis}} beforehand, dries instantly, and is preferred for patients under {{c2::6 years}}.
Neutral sodium fluoride gel is {{c1::2% or 1.1% NaF}} with a pH of about {{c2::7.0}}.
Neutral NaF gel is indicated for caries prevention, {{c1::cosmetic restorations}}, and root caries; it is ideal for patients with {{c2::xerostomia, implants, or restorations}}.
APF's {{c1::low pH}} enhances fluoride uptake.
Do not use APF on {{c1::composites, sealants, or porcelain}} — patients with cosmetic restorations (veneers, crowns, composites) should avoid it because of the risk of {{c2::etching and roughening}}.
Stannous fluoride gel is {{c1::0.4% SnF<sub>2</sub>}}; it is indicated for caries prevention, {{c2::gingivitis}}, and sensitivity.
Stannous fluoride gel may cause {{c1::extrinsic staining}} if plaque control is poor.
Silver diamine fluoride has a pH of about {{c1::8–10}} and contains {{c2::silver + ammonia}}.
SDF is indicated for hypersensitivity and {{c1::caries arrest}} in high-risk populations; it {{c2::stains carious lesions black}}.
SDF is approved for {{c1::cavity lining and sensitivity}}; its use for remineralization/caries arrest is {{c2::off-label}}.
Fluoride foam (NaF/APF) has the same concentration as the gel; there is {{c1::limited clinical evidence}} for its effectiveness, but it is still widely used.

Patients undergoing cancer therapy (especially head and neck radiation) are at high risk for {{c1::xerostomia and rampant caries}}; {{c2::fluoride varnish and prescription-strength fluoride gel}} are strongly recommended.
Orthodontic patients benefit from daily {{c1::fluoride rinses or gels}} to protect around brackets and prevent {{c2::decalcification (white spot lesions)}}.
Patients with special needs or limited dexterity may benefit from {{c1::varnish or SDF}} because of ease of application and effectiveness with minimal cooperation.
SDF is recommended for children with early childhood caries and {{c1::geriatric}} patients with limited access to {{c2::restorative care}}.
cloze.extra: Book prints 'children with early childhood' — early childhood caries.

cloze.text: {{c1::Hydroxyapatite}} is the naturally occurring mineral that makes up enamel and dentin: Ca<sub>10</sub>(PO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>6</sub>(OH)<sub>2</sub>.
Unlike fluoride, hydroxyapatite is {{c1::biomimetic}} — it mimics the natural structure of enamel and does not rely on {{c2::saliva}} to become active.

In toothpaste, {{c1::nano- or micro-hydroxyapatite}} helps rebuild enamel and fill microscopic defects: it deposits onto the enamel surface and integrates into early demineralized areas, promoting remineralization {{c2::without fluoride}}.
Some toothpastes contain {{c1::10%}} hydroxyapatite, shown to reduce {{c2::sensitivity}} and improve surface smoothness.
Hydroxyapatite is considered a {{c1::fluoride alternative}} in certain populations, e.g. {{c2::young children and fluoride-sensitive patients}}.
A night guard (occlusal guard) protects against {{c1::bruxism (grinding/clenching)}} during sleep; a sports mouthguard protects against {{c2::trauma}} during physical activity.
A night guard prevents attrition, fractures, muscle fatigue, {{c1::TMJ discomfort}}, and damage to {{c2::restorations}}.
A sports mouthguard prevents avulsion, fractures, lip/cheek lacerations, jaw injury, and {{c1::concussion}}.
Night guard materials: {{c1::hard acrylic resin}} (rigid, durable, precise fit), {{c2::soft vinyl}} (flexible, more comfortable), or {{c3::dual laminate}} (soft inside + hard outside).
Sports mouthguards are made of soft {{c1::EVA (ethylene vinyl acetate)}}; custom models may include impact gel layers or reinforcement.
Night guards come as OTC, boil-and-bite, or custom lab-fabricated; sports mouthguards come as {{c1::stock}}, boil-and-bite, or custom lab-fabricated.
Custom-fit night guard benefits: better occlusal contact, improved jaw stability, {{c1::muscle protection}}, reduced wear on restorations.
Custom-fit sports mouthguard benefits: better comfort, {{c1::improved retention}}, easier speaking and breathing, reduced {{c2::gag reflex}}.

Clean an oral guard by rinsing after use and cleaning with {{c1::mild soap, non-abrasive toothpaste, or denture tablets}}, then air-dry completely; store in a {{c2::ventilated, dry container}} to prevent fungal/bacterial growth.
cloze.extra: Same cleaning and storage for night guards and sports guards.

cloze.text: A night guard is not appropriate for patients with {{c1::severe sleep apnea}} (refer for a sleep appliance).
A sports mouthguard is not appropriate for {{c1::bruxism or nighttime use}}.

Recommend a night guard if signs of {{c1::grinding or attrition}} are observed: ask the patient, educate, and refer to the dentist. For a sports guard, ask about {{c2::sports involvement}} and recommend a custom guard.
Dental injuries make up {{c1::13–39%}} of all sports-related injuries to the face.

{{c1::Basketball and hockey}} have some of the highest rates of dental injuries, yet mouthguards are often not mandated in basketball; many {{c2::MMA and boxing}} organizations require mouthguards (no guard can disqualify a fighter).
Any oral device can accumulate plaque, calculus, materia alba, and stain; clean it in an {{c1::ultrasonic machine}} during the dental visit.
Brush a prosthesis with water, detergent, or dentifrice {{c1::after each meal and before sleeping}}; avoid overzealous brushing with strong abrasives because the material can {{c2::scratch}}.
Leave a removable prosthesis out of the mouth for some portion of each day in a {{c1::covered container with solvent}}; renew the solution with each use.
Occasionally immerse a prosthesis in a solution that removes debris; an {{c1::antifungal}} solution can be used.
Clean the {{c1::underlying mucosa}} with a soft brush to avoid oral candidiasis or lesions.
Home care around implants is essential to prevent plaque buildup, {{c1::peri-implant mucositis}}, and {{c2::peri-implantitis}}.
{{c1::Peri-implant mucositis}} is reversible inflammation of the soft tissue; untreated, it may progress to {{c2::peri-implantitis}}, which causes bone loss and implant failure.
Most implants are made of {{c1::titanium}}, which is biocompatible and supports {{c2::osseointegration}}.
Avoid metal instruments or tools directly on implant surfaces to prevent {{c1::scratching or corrosion}} of the titanium.
For implants, use a {{c1::soft-bristled, multitufted nylon}} toothbrush for gentle plaque removal.
{{c1::End-tuft and tapered}} brushes are helpful around implant abutments, prosthetics, and narrow spaces.
Power brushes (electric or sonic) are safe on implants when used with {{c1::soft bristles and gentle pressure}}.
Water flossers (oral irrigators) can reduce gingival {{c1::inflammation and bleeding}} around implants.
Around implants use interdental brushes with {{c1::nylon-coated wire cores}}; do not use {{c2::uncoated metal-core}} brushes, which can scratch the implant surface.
Implant floss options: {{c1::braided nylon floss with a built-in threader}}, spongy floss (e.g., Superfloss), and {{c2::flat cotton tape floss}} for wider contacts.
Use {{c1::floss threaders or hooks}} to access under pontics, bars, or fixed implant prostheses.
Around implants, a {{c1::rubber tip stimulator}} removes debris along the gumline and gently massages tissue; {{c2::wood sticks (e.g., Stim-U-Dent)}} may be used in wide embrasures with care.
Use an oral irrigator on implants at the {{c1::lowest pressure}} setting, with the stream directed {{c2::perpendicular to the long axis}} of the implant (not into the sulcus).
Use a {{c1::fluoridated, low-abrasive}} toothpaste on implants; avoid {{c2::whitening, charcoal, or other gritty}} pastes, which are too abrasive.
Probing depths, bleeding, and exudate around implants should be monitored {{c1::only by professionals}}; home probing is not recommended.
Advise parents to bring an infant to the dentist within {{c1::6 months}} of eruption of the first tooth or before {{c2::1 year}} of age.
For pediatric patients, provide advice on {{c1::fluoride supplementation}}.

Do not put an infant/child to bed with a bottle of formula, milk, juice, or soft drinks; {{c1::plain water}} is best for prolonged bottle use, and a {{c2::sippy cup}} should be avoided as soon as the child can drink from a cup.
A child's teeth should be brushed starting from {{c1::the appearance of the first tooth}}.
Adolescents usually respond to concerns about physical {{c1::appearance}} and peer acceptance — emphasize how damage to teeth can change appearance.
{{c1::Puberty-induced gingivitis}} and aggressive periodontitis can appear during adolescence.
cloze.extra: AAP 2017 (exam standard): 'aggressive periodontitis' is no longer a separate category — it is now periodontitis, typically grade C with a molar/incisor pattern.

cloze.text: Orthodontic appliances make home care harder: reinforce oral aids such as a {{c1::floss threader}} and proper brushing technique.
The {{c1::second}} trimester is the ideal trimester for dental treatment, but treatment can be performed anytime during pregnancy.
Essential radiographs are deemed {{c1::safe}} during pregnancy; use {{c2::ALARA}} principles to minimize exposure.
If a pregnant patient develops orthostatic hypotension (supine) in the chair, tilt her to the {{c1::left}} side.
cloze.extra: Appointments may need to be shorter; let her shift position as needed.

cloze.text: In pregnancy, caries and erosion may result from acid in {{c1::vomit}} related to morning sickness.
Maternal periodontal disease and caries may increase the risk of a {{c1::premature low-birth-weight}} infant — oral pathogens may stimulate {{c2::uterine contractions}}.
{{c1::Tetracycline}} and its derivatives are contraindicated in pregnancy to avoid intrinsic tooth staining in the fetus.
Pregnancy gingivitis: elevated {{c1::estrogen and progesterone}} exaggerate the gingival response to microorganisms; it is frequently associated with {{c2::Prevotella intermedia}}.
A {{c1::pyogenic granuloma}} (pregnancy tumor) is a localized gingival enlargement, typically involving the interdental papillae, that usually {{c2::diminishes after delivery}}.
A local anesthetic considered safe in pregnancy is {{c1::lidocaine}}.

Per the book, general anesthesia and nitrous oxide sedation are a {{c1::relative contraindication}} in pregnancy because the gas interferes with absorption of {{c2::vitamin B-12}} and other nutrients.
In pregnancy, {{c1::topical}} fluoride is recommended; there is no evidence that {{c2::systemic fluoride supplements}} taken by the mother benefit the fetus.
Restorative treatment and scaling and root planing {{c1::should be performed as needed}} during pregnancy.
Geriatric age groups: 'young old' = {{c1::65–74}}, 'old' = {{c2::75–84}}, 'old old' = {{c3::85+}}.
For geriatric patients with physical impairment, recommend {{c1::oral care aids}} such as powered toothbrushes and floss holders.
Older patients are at increased risk for periodontal diseases due to {{c1::systemic complications}} that accompany aging.
{{c1::Xerostomia}} is the most common drug-induced oral condition.
Common barriers to dental visits for older adults: {{c1::transportation}}, finances, and physical impairment.
{{c1::Mouth props (blocks)}} help patients with motor difficulty or difficulty staying open.
If a patient cannot be reclined, {{c1::elevate the patient's chair and provide care standing up}}; improvised positions must not compromise the clinician's {{c2::ergonomics}}.
cloze.extra: E.g., a wheelchair may be rotated for better comfort and access.

cloze.text: Before a wheelchair transfer, determine whether devices such as a {{c1::urine collector}} are present.
For a wheelchair transfer, set the {{c1::brake}} and lift the {{c2::footrests}}; a {{c3::sliding board}} can facilitate the transfer.
The single-provider wheelchair transfer is the {{c1::stand and pivot}} technique; use it only if the patient is {{c2::stable and partially mobile}}.
The {{c1::two-provider}} transfer is ideal for patients who cannot assist in the transfer; clear communication is essential.
In a two-provider transfer, the clinician {{c1::behind}} the patient crosses the patient's arms across the chest and grasps the wrists; the clinician {{c2::in front}} places hands under the thighs.
In a two-provider transfer, coordinate a count ("1-2-3 lift"), lift with {{c1::leg and arm muscles (not your back)}}, and lift the torso and legs {{c2::at the same time}}.
For a patient with hearing impairment, remove your mask and wear a {{c1::face shield}} so they can read lips; face the patient and speak {{c2::clearly (not louder)}}, keeping eye contact.
For hearing-impaired patients use visual tools (charts, printed instructions) and {{c1::written notes or speech-to-text apps}}.
Allow a hearing-impaired patient to {{c1::feel instruments or models}} to aid understanding, and confirm comprehension by asking them to {{c2::repeat or rephrase}} key instructions.
Use a qualified {{c1::interpreter}} if the patient uses ASL or requests assistance.
For a visually impaired patient, greet by name, {{c1::offer your arm}} for guidance, and {{c2::describe each action before doing it}}.
Keep the operatory free of obstacles and avoid {{c1::startling}} a visually impaired patient with unexpected movements or sounds.
Demonstrate home care to a visually impaired patient by letting them {{c1::touch tools and models}}; give instructions verbally or in {{c2::large print}}.
Always speak {{c1::directly to the patient}}, even if a caregiver is present.
When discussing treatment or consent with a patient who speaks another language, use {{c1::professional interpreters}}, not family or staff.
Support communication across a language barrier with simple language, {{c1::visual aids}}, or translation apps.
Translate post-op and home care instructions into the patient's {{c1::preferred language}} whenever possible.
Non-accidental bruising from abuse may take the {{c1::shape of the object}} used to hit or pinch (fingers, hands, paddle, belt buckle, teeth…).
Abuse bruising tends to occur on the buttocks, thighs, face, neck, and upper arms — usually {{c1::hidden by clothing}}.
Bruise color by age: new = {{c1::reddish-purple}}; ~1 week = {{c2::greenish}}; ~2 weeks = {{c3::yellowish}}; 2–4 weeks = {{c4::brownish}}.
cloze.extra: The book's figure labels the swatches 0 days, 1–2 days, 5–10 days, 10–14 days.

cloze.text: Oral signs of abuse: facial trauma, bruising, lacerations, bite marks, or burns in {{c1::unlikely locations}}.
{{c1::Palatal bruising}} is often associated with forced oral sex.
A torn {{c1::maxillary labial frenum}} is often associated with {{c2::forced feedings}}.
Suspected abuse: {{c1::document}} signs with pictures and ask questions of the individual believed to be at risk.
Dental professionals have a {{c1::legal duty to report}} child neglect, sexual abuse, physical harm, and emotional harm.
For {{c1::extrinsic}} stains (on the surface), start with {{c2::scaling and polishing}}; if stain persists, professional whitening may help.
For {{c1::intrinsic}} stains (within the tooth), whitening may reduce the appearance, especially in mild cases like age-related or minor trauma stains.
Deep intrinsic stains (e.g., {{c1::tetracycline, fluorosis}}) respond poorly to whitening — {{c2::veneers or bonding}} may be needed.
Always {{c1::set realistic expectations}} with the patient before starting whitening treatment.
In-office whitening uses {{c1::hydrogen peroxide}} at {{c2::15–40%}}.
At-home custom-tray whitening uses {{c1::carbamide peroxide (10–22%)}} or {{c2::hydrogen peroxide (6–12%)}}.
In-office whitening: {{c1::15–30 minutes}} per application, usually 2–3 cycles per session, ~60–90 minutes of chair time; at-home trays: {{c2::30–90 minutes}} per day, depending on product.
In-office whitening usually takes {{c1::1–2 appointments}} total; at-home tray whitening is daily use for {{c2::7–14 days}} (sometimes longer).
Shade improvement: in-office {{c1::3–8 shades}}, often visible immediately; at-home {{c2::2–5 shades}}, gradual.
Soft-tissue protection with a {{c1::resin barrier or rubber dam}} is mandatory for in-office whitening; at home it is not required, but avoid gel contact with gingiva.
Desensitizing ({{c1::KNO<sub>3</sub>}}, fluoride varnish) is often recommended before or after in-office whitening; at home, recommended if sensitivity occurs (e.g., Sensodyne).
At-home whitening is {{c1::patient-dependent}} and may have less predictable outcomes; in-office has full professional control.
{{c1::Hydrogen peroxide}} is faster acting but less stable — best for shorter wear times.
{{c1::Carbamide peroxide}} breaks down into hydrogen peroxide + {{c2::urea}} — ideal for longer, slower release (e.g., overnight trays).

basic.front: Why is fluoride varnish especially useful for patients with poor compliance?
basic.back: It does not require daily application.

basic.front: Why can school-based programs apply fluoride varnish without a prior prophylaxis?
basic.back: Fluoride can penetrate biofilm and provide protection even without full cleaning.

basic.front: Don't be confused: how does fluoride's mechanism differ from nano-hydroxyapatite's?
basic.back: Fluoride needs saliva — it is incorporated into enamel during remineralization using salivary calcium and phosphate to form fluorapatite. Nano-HAp is bioavailable in its final form and physically integrates into enamel defects on contact, even in dry or low-saliva conditions.

basic.front: Why are implants more susceptible to trauma and infection than natural teeth?
basic.back: They lack a periodontal ligament, so they have less shock absorption.

basic.front: Myth: 'the baby takes calcium from the mother's teeth.' What actually causes tooth decay during pregnancy?
basic.back: Increased acidity from morning sickness, changes in eating habits, and reduced oral hygiene from fatigue or nausea. The baby gets calcium from the mother's diet and bones — not her teeth.

basic.front: Why should a patient turn off hearing aids during ultrasonic scaling or other loud equipment?

basic.back: Confirming understanding by having the patient repeat instructions in their own words
Failure to provide adequate food, clothing, supervision, and healthcare (including dental care)

basic.front: Do most OTC 'whitening' toothpastes contain true bleaching agents? How do they work?
basic.back: No — instead of hydrogen/carbamide peroxide they use abrasives (e.g., hydrated silica, calcium carbonate) to mechanically remove extrinsic stains.

typein.question: How many minutes must fluoride gels and foams remain in the tray for effective absorption?
Acceptable implant irrigant: chlorhexidine at what concentration (%)?
typein.extra: Diluted or full strength, as prescribed.

typein.question: Typical professional recall interval for implant patients, especially with a history of periodontitis (in months)?

match.prompt: Match each dentifrice agent to its purpose.
Match each professional fluoride to its concentration.

order.prompt: Put the single-provider (stand and pivot) transfer steps in order.
items: Ensure the patient can support their weight
Secure a transfer belt around the waist (or hold the arms)
Place your feet and knees outside the patient's feet and knees
Grasp under the arms and around the back, securing the belt from the front
Pivot toward the dental chair and help them sit

sort.prompt: Sort the professional fluorides by pH.
Sort each feature: night guard or sports mouthguard?
categories: Hard acrylic, soft vinyl or dual laminate
Comes as stock, boil-and-bite or custom

sort.prompt: Sort: in-office whitening or at-home custom-tray whitening?
categories: Rubber dam or resin barrier mandatory
Best for budget-conscious, motivated patients with moderate staining

mcq.question: A 4-year-old with high caries risk is barely cooperative in the chair. Which professional fluoride is preferred?
options: A. 1.23% APF gel in trays
B. Neutral 2% NaF foam in trays
C. 5% NaF varnish
D. 0.4% SnF2 gel
mcq.answer: C. 5% NaF varnish
mcq.explanation: Varnish needs no prophylaxis, dries instantly, needs minimal cooperation and is preferred under age 6. Tray gels/foams must stay in for 4 minutes — hard for a small child and a swallowing risk.

mcq.question: A high-caries-risk adult has porcelain veneers on teeth #6–11 and several composite restorations. Which in-office fluoride should be AVOIDED?
options: A. 5% NaF varnish
B. 1.23% APF gel
C. 2% neutral NaF gel
D. Silver diamine fluoride on root caries
mcq.answer: B. 1.23% APF gel
mcq.explanation: APF's acidic pH (~3.5) can etch and roughen porcelain, composites and sealants. Neutral NaF gel (pH ~7) is the gel indicated for cosmetic restorations.

mcq.question: A patient with severe xerostomia wants a remineralizing toothpaste agent that works without relying on saliva. Which is the best choice?
options: A. Sodium fluoride
B. Nano-hydroxyapatite
C. Pyrophosphate
D. Triclosan
mcq.answer: B. Nano-hydroxyapatite
mcq.explanation: Nano-hydroxyapatite is biomimetic and integrates into enamel defects on contact, even in low-saliva conditions. Fluoride needs salivary calcium and phosphate to form fluorapatite.

mcq.question: A 16-year-old hockey player has attrition on his molars from nighttime grinding and asks whether his boil-and-bite sports guard can be worn to bed. Best response?
options: A. Yes — any guard protects teeth at night
B. No — sports guards are not appropriate for bruxism; refer to the dentist for a night guard
C. Yes, if it is cleaned with abrasive toothpaste each morning
D. No — he should stop wearing mouthguards entirely
mcq.answer: B. No — sports guards are not appropriate for bruxism; refer to the dentist for a night guard
mcq.explanation: Sports mouthguards (soft EVA) are made for trauma during activity and are not appropriate for bruxism or nighttime use. Signs of grinding → ask, educate and refer to the dentist for an occlusal (night) guard.

mcq.question: Which home-care instruction is appropriate for a patient with a new implant-supported bridge?
options: A. Use an interdental brush with an uncoated metal core
B. Direct the water flosser tip into the sulcus at high pressure
C. Use a whitening or charcoal toothpaste to prevent stain
D. Use a floss threader to clean under the fixed prosthesis
mcq.answer: D. Use a floss threader to clean under the fixed prosthesis
mcq.explanation: Floss threaders/hooks give access under pontics, bars and fixed implant prostheses. Interdental brushes must be nylon-coated, the irrigator goes on lowest pressure perpendicular to the implant (not into the sulcus), and abrasive pastes scratch titanium.

mcq.question: A patient in her 30th week of pregnancy becomes dizzy and pale while lying supine during scaling. What should the hygienist do first?
options: A. Raise the chair upright and continue
B. Turn her onto her left side
C. Administer nitrous oxide-oxygen
D. Place her in Trendelenburg and continue
mcq.answer: B. Turn her onto her left side
mcq.explanation: Supine hypotension (orthostatic hypotension) in pregnancy is relieved by tilting the patient to the left side, taking the uterus off the vena cava. Nitrous oxide is a relative contraindication per the book.

mcq.question: A patient with paraplegia cannot bear any weight and cannot assist. Which transfer is most appropriate?
options: A. Single-provider stand-and-pivot
B. Two-provider transfer
C. Have the patient stand and step into the chair
D. Treat in the wheelchair without any adjustment, regardless of ergonomics
mcq.answer: B. Two-provider transfer
mcq.explanation: The two-provider transfer is ideal for patients who cannot assist. Stand-and-pivot needs a patient who can support their weight and is stable and partially mobile.

mcq.question: A patient with limited English needs to give informed consent for scaling and root planing. Her 14-year-old son offers to translate. What should the hygienist do?
options: A. Let the son translate to save time
B. Use a professional interpreter
C. Ask a bilingual front-desk staff member
D. Give her an English consent form to sign
mcq.answer: B. Use a professional interpreter
mcq.explanation: Treatment and consent discussions need a professional interpreter, not family or staff. Afterward, confirm understanding with teach-back.

mcq.question: During an exam of a 3-year-old, the hygienist notes a torn maxillary labial frenum and bruises on the upper arms in the shape of fingers. What is the hygienist's obligation?
options: A. Ask the parent for an explanation and drop it if plausible
B. Document the findings with photos and report the suspected abuse
C. Refer the child to a pediatric dentist only
D. Note it in the chart and re-check at the next recall
mcq.answer: B. Document the findings with photos and report the suspected abuse
mcq.explanation: A torn maxillary labial frenum (forced feeding) and patterned bruising suggest abuse. Dental professionals have a legal duty to report suspected child abuse/neglect and should document the signs with pictures.

mcq.question: A patient wants her teeth whitened as much as possible before her wedding in 5 days. Which option best fits?
options: A. OTC whitening toothpaste
B. At-home trays with 10% carbamide peroxide
C. In-office whitening with 15–40% hydrogen peroxide
D. Porcelain veneers
mcq.answer: C. In-office whitening with 15–40% hydrogen peroxide
mcq.explanation: In-office whitening gives 3–8 shades, often visible immediately, in 1–2 appointments — best for fast, pre-event results. At-home trays need 7–14 days for a gradual 2–5 shade change.

mcq.question: A patient says she brushes once daily and snacks frequently on sugary drinks. She has generalized interproximal caries. Which is the most appropriate initial education topic?
options: A. Flossing technique
B. Brushing with an electric toothbrush
C. Frequency and type of sugar intake
D. The use of water flossers
mcq.answer: C. Frequency and type of sugar intake
mcq.explanation: Dietary counseling takes priority when caries risk is high due to frequent sugar. (Keywords: snacks frequently, sugary drinks, most appropriate.)

mcq.question: Which risk factor most increases a patient's risk for periodontal disease?
options: A. Smoking one pack of cigarettes per day
B. Brushing once daily
C. Consuming high amounts of sugar
D. Lack of flossing
mcq.answer: A. Smoking one pack of cigarettes per day
mcq.explanation: Smoking is the #1 modifiable risk factor for periodontal disease. (Exam standard: record smoking as cigarettes per day — 1 pack = 20 cigarettes.)

mcq.question: A high caries risk patient declines fluoride treatment due to cultural beliefs. What is the most appropriate response by the dental hygienist?
options: A. Educate the patient using current evidence-based research and strongly encourage fluoride use to reduce caries
B. Respect the patient's decision, but document the refusal
C. Acknowledge the patient's perspective, offer education on fluoride and alternative options, and document their acceptance or refusal
D. Emphasize the importance of fluoride and recommend the patient reconsider at the next visit
mcq.answer: C. Acknowledge the patient's perspective, offer education on fluoride and alternative options, and document their acceptance or refusal
mcq.explanation: The most ethical and culturally competent approach respects autonomy while offering non-coercive education. It preserves the patient-provider relationship and aligns with informed consent. Simply pushing evidence without regard for belief systems may come off as dismissive or culturally insensitive.

mcq.question: Which brushing method is commonly recommended for a patient with orthodontic brackets?
options: A. Bass
B. Stillman
C. Charter's
D. Fone's
mcq.answer: C. Charter's
mcq.explanation: Charter's method directs bristles away from the gingiva and toward the occlusal/incisal edge, making it ideal for cleaning around brackets, prosthetics, or post-surgical areas.

mcq.question: A 5-year-old child presents for their first hygiene appointment. Which brushing method would be most appropriate to teach the caregiver?
options: A. Modified Bass
B. Fone's
C. Stillman
D. Charter's
mcq.answer: B. Fone's
mcq.explanation: Fone's method uses large circular motions, which are easier for children or caregivers to perform and understand. It's often used in pediatric or special needs cases, though not ideal for adults.

mcq.question: A patient with a fixed bridge and type II embrasures is struggling to maintain interproximal hygiene. Which aid should you recommend?
options: A. Unwaxed floss
B. Wooden wedge
C. Tufted dental floss
D. End-tuft brush
mcq.answer: C. Tufted dental floss
mcq.explanation: Tufted floss is ideal for cleaning under bridges and in type II or III embrasures, thanks to its thicker, yarn-like texture and ability to adapt to wider spaces and irregular surfaces.

mcq.question: Which interdental aid would be most suitable for a patient with reduced manual dexterity and tight contacts?
options: A. Floss threader
B. Waxed floss with a floss handle
C. Interdental brush
D. Wooden wedge
mcq.answer: B. Waxed floss with a floss handle
mcq.explanation: A floss handle aids patients with poor dexterity, and waxed floss glides more easily through tight contacts, improving comfort and effectiveness.

mcq.question: A patient with Parkinson's disease is scheduled for dental hygiene care. Which clinical consideration is MOST appropriate?
options: A. Stabilize instruments and protect the airway during treatment
B. Avoid caregiver involvement to promote independence
C. Allow for longer appointments due to frequent bathroom breaks
D. Recommend an alcohol-based mouthrinse for home care
mcq.answer: A. Stabilize instruments and protect the airway during treatment
mcq.explanation: Parkinson's patients may have tremors and difficulty controlling muscle movement. Stabilizing instruments and airway protection help prevent aspiration and injury during care.

mcq.question: A patient taking Elavil® (a tricyclic antidepressant) presents for scaling and root planing. What local anesthetic modification is recommended?
options: A. Administer lidocaine with 0.2 mg epinephrine
B. Use only topical anesthetics
C. Delay treatment until medication is discontinued
D. Avoid levonordefrin-containing anesthetics like Mepivacaine®
mcq.answer: D. Avoid levonordefrin-containing anesthetics like Mepivacaine®
mcq.explanation: Tricyclic antidepressants can interact negatively with levonordefrin, increasing cardiovascular risk. Epinephrine can be used in low doses, but levonordefrin should be avoided.

mcq.question: A 56-year-old patient experienced a stroke two months ago. What is the most appropriate course of action?
options: A. No modifications required
B. Postpone elective dental treatment until 6 months post-attack
C. Administer supplemental oxygen while treating the patient
D. Patient should stop blood thinner prior to appointment to reduce risk of excessive bleeding
mcq.answer: B. Postpone elective dental treatment until 6 months post-attack
mcq.explanation: Dental treatment should be postponed for at least 6 months after a stroke to reduce risk of complications, particularly with invasive procedures.

mcq.question: A patient presents with pinpoint pupils during the dental appointment. Which substance is most likely responsible for this clinical sign?
options: A. Cocaine
B. Heroin
C. Methamphetamine
D. Alcohol
mcq.answer: B. Heroin
mcq.explanation: Pinpoint pupils (miosis) are a classic sign of opioid use such as heroin, morphine, codeine, fentanyl, methadone, and oxycodone. Cocaine causes dilated pupils (mydriasis), while methamphetamine and alcohol do not typically cause miosis.
